title: An interfaith service
hookLine: Guru Tegh Bahadur's day as a time to stand for others' freedom
tomorrow: a new month starts tomorrow. what do you read first?

lines: WHY DIE FOR PEOPLE NOT SIKH?
cards: The folding chairs in the gurdwara hall are mixed today. Mrs. Haddad from next door, in her good coat.
Maya's grandmother with a Bible in her lap. A few people from the mosque down the road and the temple across town.
The gurdwara has invited its neighbors for Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom day, and Simran is at the microphone with three lines on a card and hands that won't stay still.
Then a man near the back asks it out loud: why would your Guru die for people who weren't even Sikh?

teach.b: Here's the story Sikhs tell. Pandits from Kashmir came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur, under pressure from the emperor's officials to give up their faith.
Tradition says the Guru listened, then went to Delhi himself, knowing what it might cost. He was arrested, and in the square at Chandni Chowk he was put to death. Gurdwara Sis Ganj stands there now.
He didn't share their faith. He didn't wear their sacred thread or their tilak, the mark on the forehead. His son, Guru Gobind Singh, wrote that his father protected their tilak and their thread.

teach.h: HIND DI CHADAR: A SHELTERING CLOTH.
teach.b: That's why Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar: the sheet, the covering of India, the cloth you'd put over someone to shelter them.

teach.h: FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.
teach.b: His own verses in the Guru Granth Sahib describe a person like that: bhai kaahoo kau det neh, neh bhai maanat aan. One who frightens no one, and is afraid of no one. So a service with neighbors on his day isn't an extra.
It's the point of the day: standing up for someone else's right to pray in their own way. Simran reads her three lines. Her hands stop shaking somewhere in the second one.

how: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom day with kirtan of his hymns, Ardas and langar, and some visit Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi; some gurdwaras invite neighbors of other faiths to gatherings on freedom of belief.

o: a debate where faiths argue over which is right
a ceremony that blends everyone's prayers into one
neighbors of many faiths honoring each one's freedom

games.q: the ninth Guru's day — tap the pairs.
p: came to Anandpur asking for help
the square where he was put to death
what his son says he protected

s: Guru Tegh Bahadur died defending Sikhs' right to worship
the Kashmiri Pandits who came to him weren't Sikh; he stood for their freedom.
Hind di Chadar means the covering, the shelter, of India
a chadar is a sheet, the cloth you put over someone to shelter them.
his verses describe one who frightens no one and fears no one
bhai kaahoo kau det neh, neh bhai maanat aan, on Ang 1427.

games.q: at the service, someone says Guru Tegh Bahadur taught that every religion is the same, so he defended them all. what's the fair correction?
o: he didn't wear their thread or tilak; he stood for their freedom to keep a faith not his own.
it's right: he gave his life to prove all religions teach the same thing.
he was defending the Sikh community's land from the emperor.
games.why: the story's force is the difference: he didn't share their faith, and he stood for their freedom anyway. that's why Sikhs call him Hind di Chadar.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one neighbor, coworker or classmate whose faith or way of life isn't yours. Hold them there, along with their freedom to be who they are.
If you pray, you can pray for peace between your neighbors and you; if not, simply wish them well, and stay with them till the bell.

wordCard.voice: An interfaith service. Neighbors of different faiths gathering on Guru Tegh Bahadur's day to honor each one's freedom to worship.

orig.note: Punjabi: the sheet, the covering of India, a title Sikhs give Guru Tegh Bahadur.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: freedom for all, even for a faith you don't share. Simran got through all three lines.
